title: A sabbath
hook: a day, or a piece of one, set apart
tomorrow: who in your life gets the real answer to "how are you"?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunday worship: a room in Troas nobody wanted to leave. Your line was gather. Today, the week's other gift: stopping.

The laptop opens on the couch just for ten minutes, and suddenly it's dark out. Saturday goes to catching up, Sunday to errands, and the week never really ends; it just starts over. The Bible's answer to that isn't a better system. It's a day, set apart, where the unfinished stays unfinished on purpose. Christians agree the day is a gift. They don't all agree which day it is.
screen: `JUST TEN MINUTES.` → `THE WEEK NEVER ENDS.` → `A DAY. BUT WHICH ONE?`

segments.voice: It starts with God, not with a rule. Genesis says: “And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.” Later, at Sinai, it becomes a command: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.” Now the two views. Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. Their best case is simple: the commandment names the seventh day, God blessed that day, and no verse moves it. For them, the date itself is part of the keeping. Other Christians keep Sunday as the Lord's day of worship and rest, the day of the resurrection, and some read Paul as leaving the day itself open: “One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.” Their best case: the gift is the rest, not the date, and the rest grew out of gathering on the morning of the resurrection. Both sides read the same Bible carefully. And both lean on one scene in Mark. Jesus' hungry disciples pick grain on the sabbath, someone asks why, and he answers: “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.” Whatever the day, the stopping is a gift. That's the part they share.

segments.voice: Set your phone face down, out of reach. Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, the posture of someone who isn't making anything right now. Stay there, and choose one stretch this week, an evening or a morning, that you'll guard the same way. If you pray, you can open that stretch with Genesis in mind: God resting, and calling the day blessed.
A sabbath. A day, or a piece of one, set apart: blessed by God in Genesis, commanded at Sinai, and made for people.
Your line: rest is holy. God rested first, and then blessed the day. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians keep a weekly day of rest and worship in different ways: some keep Sunday as the Lord's Day, Seventh-day Adventists and some others keep Saturday, and some set apart another day or evening when work makes Sunday impossible.

fork.setup: your Adventist friend keeps Saturday; you keep Sunday. she asks you to say her side at its strongest. what do you say?
options: the commandment names the seventh day, and no verse moves it.

fork.reveal: her best case is the text itself: God blessed the seventh day, and Sinai says remember the sabbath day. the Sunday side's best case is Paul's freedom about days and the resurrection.

chat.says: dad works 24-hour shifts, so our family rest day moves every week. does a moving sabbath even count?
options: Christians differ on the day, but it was made for people. A guarded rest counts.
Only if it's Sunday. Any other day is just a day off, not a real sabbath.
Rest is optional now. Jesus set the old sabbath aside, so it doesn't matter.
chat.meaning: Adventists keep Saturday, others keep Sunday, and Paul lets each be persuaded. Mark's line holds for all: the sabbath was made for man.

Sinai.meaning: the mountain where Israel receives the commandments in Exodus

Seventh-day Adventists.meaning: a Protestant church that keeps Saturday as the sabbath

the Lord's day.meaning: an early Christian name for Sunday, the day of the resurrection
